hook_text: In South African cities, a mansion and a shack can be only a few kilometres apart. Why?
clip_script: Most of a city's land is homes. In high-income suburbs: big plots, gardens, pools, low density. In middle-income areas: smaller houses, townhouses, flats. In low-income areas: small houses packed close, and informal settlements with shared taps. But income is only half the story. In 1950 the Group Areas Act divided every city by race. District Six. Sophiatown. Cato Manor. Families forced out. White suburbs near the centre. Townships far away, behind buffer zones of railways and open land, with few shops or parks. Since 1994 anyone can live anywhere. But good land costs money, so the old map is still there. Income plus history: that is the unequal city.
visual_style: A whiteboard bird's-eye view of a city with large green plots on one side and densely packed roofs on the other, separated by a railway buffer, then a stamp reading Group Areas Act 1950.
pacing: Steady comparison, slowing for the history.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn how to read residential areas on maps.
